transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-27 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes

Attendees:
- Emma Carter (Redwood AE)
- Ravi Patel (Redwood SE)
- Jules Moreno (Redwood CSM)
- Maya Chen (Oryx SRE)
- Aaron Lopez (Oryx VP Eng)
- Dina Park (Oryx CTO)
- Samir Nadeem (Oryx Backend Lead)

Summary:
Brief postmortem follow-up on the 2026-03-20 throughput/latency regression that impacted Oryx storefront recommendation calls. Focus on root cause hypoth, autoscaler behavior, KV cache interactions, and a remediation playbook including a dedicated pilot.

Topics:
- incident timeline and observed client impact
- autoscaler misfire and cold-start surge
- KV cache eviction/leak suspicion
- routing fallbacks and degraded model variants
- proposed hotfixes and pilot scope
- observability gaps and long term hardenings

Transcript:
[00:00] Emma Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. we wanted to walk through our early findings from the regression last week and agree on the remediation plan. ravi, do you want to kick off with timeline?
[00:22] Ravi Patel: yeah sure, um so quick recap — on 2026-03-20 between 13:40 and 14:15 UTC we saw a spike in tail latency on the recommendations route. tokenized per-request latency went from a 95th of ~120ms to uh 850ms for a period of about 20 minutes, and error rates bumped where fallback started triggering.
[00:45] Maya Chen: yep that's what we saw, many of our frontend requests started timing out at 10s and then fell back to cached results which degraded UX. we also saw a big queue depth increase on the inference hosts.
[01:05] Aaron Lopez: For context, uptime was fine but the user-visible slowness cost us conversion in that window so we need both root cause and guardrails.
[01:18] Ravi Patel: Absolutely. early indicators point to two compounding issues: our autoscaler decision loop reacted late to a pattern of many short-lived, high-concurrency sessions; meanwhile there was a KV cache eviction pattern that caused model hot paths to recompile/reattach which amplified cold-start token overhead.
[01:45] Samir Nadeem: excuse me, when you say KV cache, do you mean the prefix/KV cache that's stored in the serving layer or your redis cache?
[01:55] Ravi Patel: good call — it's the serving KV cache, local to the GPU worker. we observed unusually large KV-resize operations in the logs around the same time as the autoscaler events. the logs sometimes transcribed as "KV cahce" in earlier notes, ha.
[02:20] Maya Chen: we also had a misconfigured horizontal autoscaler policy in our private deployment; the scale-up threshold was set too conservatively because of a legacy knob. so nodes were added but not fast enough for the burst.
[02:40] Dina Park: can you clarify whether the fallback routing to smaller models contributed? we had the system fall back to a cheaper, smaller variant and that looked like it actually made things worse in terms of latency.
[02:57] Ravi Patel: yeah that was surprising — the fallback route had a different batching profile and caused more synchronous CPU/PU contention. in short, fallback isn't always cheaper end-to-end.
[03:15] Emma Carter: again the combinatorics here — autoscale delay + cache thrash + fallback mismatch — is what stacked the triangle of badness.
[03:28] Aaron Lopez: what about request patterns? were there bursts from cron jobs or a client-side retry storm?
[03:35] Maya Chen: we traced a spike to an A/B test rollout that increased candidate set size for some traffic buckets; that wasn't communicated in the rollout notes so it blindsided the autoscaler.
[03:50] Ravi Patel: ok that helps explain the short-lived high concurrency. so immediate mitigations we propose: 1) tune autoscaler to be more reactive for short bursts using a hybrid metric (queue depth + 95th latency), 2) patch the KV cache eviction thresholds to avoid massive resizes, 3) change fallback policy to prefer model variants with compatible batching profiles, and 4) add a short-term dedicated capacity pilot to absorb similar bursts.
[04:20] Emma Carter: ravi, can you outline the patch sequence and risk?
[04:25] Ravi Patel: of course — minimal hotfix is a config change to autoscaler target and lower scale-up cooldown, low risk and reversible. KV cache threshold change is a runtime param we can flip, small risk but we want to monitor memory footprint. fallback policy change requires config + a canary rollout since it affects routing decisions. dedicated pilot is separate — we'll provision a small reserved pool and route a slice of traffic for a week.
[04:55] Samir Nadeem: how do you propose we validate the KV fix? we can't reproduce perfectly in staging.
[05:03] Ravi Patel: good point — we'll use controlled soak tests with synthetic sessions that mimic the A/B candidate size pattern; also capture and replay sampled request traces into the pilot. we may need a short-lived feature flag in prod for safe canarying.
[05:25] Maya Chen: about telemetry — we need better signal. our ops runbooks missed the early signs. what additional metrics do you need from us?
[05:33] Ravi Patel: queue depth per host, KV-resize events, per-model batching latency breakdown, and autoscaler decision timestamps. if you can export those to a shared bucket we can pull them into our dashboards.
[05:50] Emma Carter: we'll prepare an incident timeline slide and include a minimal telemetry export format we need.
[05:57] Aaron Lopez: on the pilot — what's the expected cost delta? our finance team wants a ballpark before approving.
[06:05] Emma Carter: rough numbers — for the pilot sized to handle 2x the observed peak you'd be looking at a one-week dedicated pool that's about 15-20% of your monthly inference spend; we'll provide a precise quote in the follow-up.
[06:20] Dina Park: ok send the quote. also, security — would pilot require additional onboarding for our on-prem KMS?
[06:28] Ravi Patel: pilot can run in your VPC with existing KMS integration; there may be an ops checklist but no new long-term keys. we'll share the KMS integration doc.
[06:40] Emma Carter: action items recap — we'll send RCA slides, PR for autoscaler, sample traces request, and the dedicated pilot proposal. any objections?
[06:50] Maya Chen: none, just please include clear rollback steps for each change.
[06:55] Ravi Patel: will do. wanted to flag two lower-priority long-term hardenings too: better canarying around fallback policy and per-tenant pre-warming for models with large KV footprints.
[07:12] Samir Nadeem: whats the timeline for the autoscaler patch?
[07:16] Ravi Patel: I can open the PR today, target ship to canary by Monday 2026-03-29, and monitor for a few days before wider roll.
[07:25] Aaron Lopez: ok Monday works.
[07:30] Emma Carter: let's talk through the telemetry we need — maya, can you share the location of your metrics and an example export format?
[07:40] Maya Chen: sure we'll give you a read-only bucket with TF-compatible traces and a metrics slice for the problem window.
[07:48] Jules Moreno: i'll coordinate the pilot logistics and budget sign-off path, and liaise with finance.
[07:55] Dina Park: one more question — any dependency on model changes? i.e. do we need to retrain or is this purely infra/config?
[08:03] Ravi Patel: mostly infra/config. there is a small optimization in the model variant packaging that would reduce cold-start size but that's not in the critical path for the next week.
[08:15] Maya Chen: what about alerting? we had alerts for error rate but not for queue depth or KV-resize anomalies.
[08:22] Emma Carter: agreed add queue depth and KV-resize spikes to alerting, with a low-noise threshold.
[08:30] Aaron Lopez: do we have an estimate on user impact (lost revenue) for that 20-minute window?
[08:37] Maya Chen: preliminary estimate is ~0.6% conversion loss for that window across affected buckets; we'll refine and share in the RCA.
[08:45] Ravi Patel: ok wrapping up — immediate next steps: PR for autoscaler (Ravi), RCA slides + telemetry spec (Emma), sample traces and metric access (Maya), pilot budget sign-off (Dina/Aaron).
[09:00] Emma Carter: perfect. we'll target the follow-up check-in after the PR lands and pilot is scoped — propose 2026-03-31 for a 30-minute sync.
[09:12] Aaron Lopez: that works. thanks everyone.
[09:18] Dina Park: thanks.

End of transcript.
